title: Safe distancing in the time of COVID-19
contribution: Joint with Martina Fischetti (first author, whose wind-farm layout MILP and matheuristic are reused) and Stoustrup: recasts table, umbrella and seat placement under COVID-19 distancing as wind-farm layout with virus-spread interference, compares five interference forms on toy layouts, fits more facilities than manual layouts on real cases (36 vs 30 tables, 211 vs 203 umbrellas), and draws the lesson that the safest layouts load the border instead of spacing facilities equally.
problem_entry: Distancing rules make businesses place tables or seats under a minimum distance; the cited OR work packs or assigns seats (MILP, p-dispersion, circle packing); entry: fix the number of facilities, minimize total infection risk, and test the intuition that maximal equal spacing is safest, via the parallel with offshore wind-farm layout (pp. 2-7).
key_idea: Read wake interference as virus-spread interference and reuse the wind-farm MILP unchanged (binaries on sampled positions, conflict rows for d_ij < Dmin, one aggregated continuous w_i per position with big-M M_i), expressing each variant as data: maximum packing with Nmin = 0, Nmax = +inf, P_i = 10^3; a fixed count with Nmin = Nmax; family groups as configuration variables with per-size cardinality rows (pp. 7-9, 15, 17, 20-21).
assumptions: 0-1 location with a cardinality row, conflict-edge packing rows and big-M linking rows; risk additive over pairs, I_ij an input left to the decision maker in five forms (linear d_max - d, Gaussian sigma^2 = 1, 1/d, 1/d^1.5, 1/d^3); constant factors irrelevant to the optimum; toy runs with Dmin = 0, P_i = 0, Nmin = Nmax = k; theatre model with 506 configurations and 11,726 forbidden pairs (pp. 8-11, 20-22).
proof_devices: No proof. Degenerate-optimum check: under the linear form (9), 3 facilities on a segment put two at the endpoints and the third anywhere at the same value, so (9) is rejected, p. 10
Single-index aggregation credited to Fischetti and Monaci 2016: one continuous w_i per position with big-M M_i = sum of I_ij over compatible j instead of two-index variables, pp. 8-9
Configuration variables for family groups with precomputed incompatible pairs and per-size cardinality rows (14), pp. 20-21
experiments: Illustrations, not a benchmark: 10 facilities on a line and 20 in a 10 m square under five risk forms (induced minimum distances 2.57/1.80/2.40/2.50 m for (10)-(13); 1/d^k for k in {1.5, 2, 3} gives essentially the same layout); real cases against practitioner layouts: 36 vs 30 tables at a Copenhagen brewpub, 211 vs 203 umbrellas on a Venice beach, a tables-versus-risk Pareto curve; theatre model size only; no solver, hardware, run time, gap or seed reported (pp. 11-21).
positioning: Adds a risk objective to distancing work that packs or assigns seats (Salari et al., Kudela's p-dispersion, Pavlik et al., Ugail et al.'s circle packing, Moore et al.) and imports the first author's wind-farm layout optimizer; leaves the choice of interference form to epidemiologists and virologists (pp. 3-4, 7-10, 22).
writing: Picture-first hook (two 20-facility layouts in Fig. 1) and a rhetorical test of intuition (p. 4); a lesson learned closes the abstract (p. 2); the disclaimer on the interference form is repeated in Sections 4 and 6 (pp. 10, 22); limitations get their own paragraphs (pp. 21-22).
limits_future: Counter-intuitive layouts are hard to explain to a non-technical audience (p. 21); pairwise-additive risk excludes risk that is nonlinear in the whole layout (p. 22); no answer on the right interference form (pp. 10, 22); future: direction-dependent interference from air conditioning or Plexiglas (p. 21).

method_links.note: Weak and joint; the model is credited to the first author's 2016 paper with Monaci: one aggregated continuous variable per position replaces two-index interference variables, kept because it solves larger instances.

The machinery tried first is an existing MILP model plus matheuristic from another application, reused unchanged; new variants are data (P_i, Nmin, Nmax, Dmin) or a change of what a binary stands for (configurations), not new code; no plain-solver run on the plain model is reported.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Toy-instance check of a modelling choice
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A candidate interference form is rejected because the smallest instance with an obvious answer (3 facilities on a segment) has a degenerate optimum; the surviving forms are compared on 10 points on a line and 20 in a square before any real case.

transferable: Before trusting a penalty or interference function, solve the smallest instance whose right answer you know and drop forms whose optimum is degenerate there (3 facilities on a segment, p. 10); then compare the survivors on 1-D and 2-D toy layouts (pp. 11-14).
Model pairwise interference with one continuous variable per location and one big-M row, M_i = sum of I_ij over the compatible j, instead of one variable per pair (pp. 8-9).

Express problem variants as data of one model: maximum count with Nmin = 0, Nmax = +inf and a large P_i (10^3) (p. 15); a fixed count with Nmin = Nmax (p. 17); Dmin = 0 and P_i = 0 to see what the objective alone does (p. 11).
For grouped entities (families), let each binary stand for a feasible configuration, precompute the incompatible pairs, and add one cardinality row per group size (pp. 20-21).
Drop constant factors from the objective so the optimum does not depend on parameters nobody knows, and test robustness to the functional form (1/d^k for k in {1.5, 2, 3}) (pp. 10, 14).
Compare with the layout the practitioner actually uses, on the same area and rule (203 against 211 umbrellas at 4 m) (p. 18).
coauthors: Martina Fischetti (Vattenfall BA Wind, first author), Jakob Stoustrup (Aalborg University)

quotes.text: The intuition would tell us that, placing facilities at the maximum distance one from each other would ensure the safest layout. But is this really the case?
using a single index variable wi allows this model to solve larger instances compared with equivalent two-index models in the literature

title: Thinning out facilities: a Benders decomposition approach for the uncapacitated facility location problem with separable convex costs
contribution: The April 2015 report version of the Benders facility-location work (journal version S011): projects the allocation variables of UFL and separable convex quadratic UFL out with (generalized) Benders cuts in a CPLEX 12.6 branch-and-cut, stabilizes the root cut loop with a simple in-out scheme against the curse of Kelley, solves 7 open UFLLIB instances, improves 22 best-known values and speeds qUFL up by up to four orders of magnitude, with the numbers the 2016 preprint reports.
problem_entry: Allocation variables make UFL hard for MILP solvers, so Lagrangian methods are preferred; the thinning out of the Steiner-tree work is transferred to UFL, and Benders for linear UFL is folklore forgotten for 30+ years; a sound Lagrangian code is far from trivial, hence a simpler approach on a stock solver (pp. 1-2, 6, 26).
key_idea: Remove x_ij and bound one w_j per customer (fat) or one w_sum (slim) by GB cuts separated in a stock branch-and-cut; the cure for slow convergence is the loop, not the cut: in-out stabilization at the root, derived from the analogy with Lagrangian dual minimization, Kelley kept in the tree (pp. 5, 12-17).
assumptions: UFL with c_ij >= 0 (infinite if forbidden) and qUFL with unit demands and c_ij > 0, compact baseline the perspective SOC model; master with at least 2 open facilities (1- and 2-facility solutions enumerated for linear n <= 1000); GB cuts need convex twice-differentiable slaves and constraint qualifications; the QP derivation assumes y* > 0; data UFLLIB M* and KG, Barahona-Chudak, ORLIB (zero costs 1e-5), random qUFL up to 2000 x 10000 (pp. 3-6, 8, 20-21, 23).
proof_devices: Generalized Benders cut from Geoffrion's sensitivity formula (18), explained through the Lagrangian at the optimal multipliers, p. 6
Linear slave as a continuous knapsack: Dantzig's critical item gives primal and dual in closed form, so only n distinct Benders cuts exist per customer, pp. 7-8

Perspective costs gamma_i = c_i / y*_i after eliminating z; Algorithm 1 (clip violated bounds, re-solve the residual problem) proved by Lemma 2.1 (beta strictly increasing) and Theorem 2.1 (KKT check), pp. 9-12
Fat and slim masters have the same bound, being projections of one formulation on different w-subspaces; the cumulative cut is implied a la Farkas, p. 13
Single aggregated optimality cut (43) for integer master points in the lazy callback, p. 19

Numerical safeguards: perspective strengthening skipped for y*_i < 1e-5 or > 1 - 1e-5; separation at y* + 2 epsilon keeps cuts valid; EPINT = 0, EPGAP and EPRHS 1e-9; Margot-style validity test repeated 10,000 times, pp. 13-14, 20
experiments: CPLEX 12.6, Xeon E3-1220V2 3.10 GHz 16 GB, wall-clock, 4 threads, basic untuned settings; single-thread traces on gs250a-1 (same separator under Kelley, Kelley+ and in-out; fat: Kelley stopped at the root after 15,000 s, in-out root 0.19 s and done at 0.41 s; slim: in-out root 0.04 s with 4 cuts) and fat vs slim on MT1; linear: 7 open UFLLIB instances solved (2500-10 in 824.76 s), 22 best-known values improved and 22 matched by four seeded single-thread local-branching runs; qUFL: up to four orders of magnitude over the perspective model (MIQCPSTRAT = 1), which runs out of memory from n, m >= 200; slim beats fat at scale with root gaps under 0.04%; all KG qUFL solved; no exact-run time limit and no timing seeds stated; per-instance results in an online appendix (pp. 15-28).
positioning: Against the Lagrangian state of the art (Posta et al.'s cooperative method, Beltran-Royo et al.'s semi-Lagrangian relaxation) through solved status and best-known values; Benders credited to Magnanti-Wong and Cornuejols-Nemhauser-Wolsey as forgotten folklore; in-out credited to Ben-Ameur-Neto and Fischetti-Salvagnin only (the 2016 version widens the list, per card S011); thinning out credited to the Steiner-tree paper (pp. 2-4, 6, 15, 21).
writing: Twofold outcome stated up front (p. 2); the argument carried by section titles on the curse of Kelley and on slim or fat (pp. 14, 17); candid asides (MIP people's Pavlov's aversion to aggregated formulations, resisting the temptation, to our big surprise) (pp. 13-14, 23); the key ingredient flagged in so many words (p. 14); the QP routine proved so that results can be reproduced (p. 9).
limits_future: No real bundle method (p. 15); Kelley kept in the tree since a better loop inside CPLEX is not immediate (p. 17); for linear costs the root bound is not tight, so many nodes (p. 18); 50 KG linear instances still out of reach (p. 21); capacitated FL not immediate; future: connected FL, ring-star, median cycle, traveling purchaser, convex MINLP solvers, nonlinear stochastic programming (pp. 27-28).

method_links.note: Same paper as S011, not independent: thinning out transferred from the Steiner-tree work, x_ij projected out, w_j aggregated into w_sum with the same-bound projection argument against the aversion to aggregated formulations, fat or slim chosen per cost class by measurement.

Dated to April 2015: section 3.2 blames Kelley's loop rather than cut strength (the curse of Kelley), derives the cure from the Lagrangian-dual analogy, runs one separator under three policies on gs250a-1 with the numbers of the 2016 preprint (so the showcase instance dates from this report), and keeps stabilization at the root because a better loop inside CPLEX is not immediate; lineage credit [5, 12] only.

A quick shot: one GB separator plugged into CPLEX 12.6 already solved open instances; a simple in-out variant instead of a bundle method; no qUFL heuristics because none were needed; his local branching and proximity search reused as sub-MIP heuristics. Ingredients were then added for much better results, and only the loop and the fat or slim choice are ablated.

Partial: the compact perspective baseline runs with the CPLEX option that suits it best (MIQCPSTRAT = 1), the new code with basic untuned settings; linear-case comparisons via solved status and best-known values from the literature, not a common harness.
Seeds only as a resource (four concurrent seeded single-thread runs, best solution kept); no seeds or repetitions are reported for the timing results.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Reframe for the venue, keep the evidence
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Between this April 2015 report and the February 2016 preprint (S011) the title changes (S011 p. 1); a text search of the S011 file finds neither the Steiner-tree entry nor the curse-of-Kelley or folklore wording; the motivation becomes big data and sleeping beauties (S011 p. 2); the in-out lineage widens (card S011, D6); the numbers stay the same. One pair only; the skill's Workflow F lists draft revision as not documented.

transferable: When a cut loop stalls, ask whether the master LP is a known problem in disguise and borrow that field's stabilization: minimizing a convex function over the 0-1 box is Lagrangian dual minimization, where bundle methods beat Kelley, so a simple in-out loop replaces Kelley at the root (pp. 14-15).

Before any table, compare loop policies with the same separator on one instance, on a log time axis with cut counts at the end of the root and of the run: Kelley, Kelley separating at y* + 2 epsilon, in-out (pp. 15-17).

In-out constants and reset schedule: stabilizer at all ones, moved halfway each iteration; separate at lambda y* + (1 - lambda) y~ + delta (1,...,1) with lambda = 0.2 and delta = 2 epsilon; lambda = 1 after 5 iterations without bound improvement, delta = 0 after 5 more, stop and drop slack cuts after 5 more; drop slack cuts every 5th iteration (p. 15).

When only the sum of per-customer costs matters, aggregate them into one variable, argue that the bound is unchanged because both masters project the same formulation, then choose fat or slim per cost class by measurement (pp. 12-13, 17-18).
If the Benders slave is a continuous knapsack, write the cut in closed form from the critical item: only n distinct cuts exist per customer, and the model stays compact (pp. 2, 7-8).

Stress-test the cut generator after each run: fix the incumbent, perturb 80% of its entries by 1e-9 to 1e-1, separate, add the cuts statically, re-solve, 10,000 times, and write the model to a file on infeasibility (p. 20).
coauthors: Ivana Ljubić, Markus Sinnl (University of Vienna)

quotes.text: Recent experience with the Steiner Tree Problem [9] showed that some known MILP models can be “thinned out” by removing unnecessary variables and constraints, with a very significant performance boost.
Evidently, one can design a sound cutting plane loop even with very weak/dense cuts, provided that the “Kelley’s curse” is escaped and a different cutting plane scheme is adopted.
